We have carbon NMR data: list of chemical shifts (duplicate pairs likely due to symmetry). Need number of methyl groups (CH3). Methyl carbon typically around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, maybe 20-30. In data we have peaks at 19.40 (duplicate) and 34.50 (duplicate) and 62.10 (duplicate) and aromatic region 124-135. So likely methyl carbon at 19.40 ppm (typical). 34.5 could be CH2 or tertiary carbon. 62 could be O-CH2. So number of methyl groups likely 1 (one CH3). But need confirm if there are two equivalent methyls giving one peak (duplicate due to symmetry). The carbon NMR shows each carbon appears twice? Actually duplicates maybe because of two identical carbons? For example, if there are two methyl groups chemically equivalent, they'd give one signal, not duplicate. Duplicate could be due to two distinct but similar carbons? But carbon NMR normally shows each unique carbon; duplicates indicate symmetry? Actually if there are two equivalent carbons, they give one signal. Duplicate signals could be due to two different carbons with same shift (coincident). But likely the sample has two methyl groups with same shift? Could be isopropyl? But 19.4 typical for methyl attached to aromatic? Could be two methyls on aromatic ring (toluene groups) giving same shift. However aromatic methyls appear around 20-25 ppm. So 19.4 could be methyl attached to aromatic ring. If there are two such methyls, they'd be equivalent if para? Might give one signal. But we need count of methyl groups, not unique signals.

We need more info: maybe get proton NMR to see methyl protons. Let's retrieve proton NMR.
